A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TABLET research work. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, equations, and figures are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions in v3.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning experiments, held-in and held-out evaluations, and ablations comparing visualization styles, dataset sizes, and task inclusion.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds VisualTableQA evaluations, Gemma 3 fine-tuning results, and performance analyses by visual complexity.

M1.justification: The core TABLET retrieval, rendering, highlighting, and instruction-construction pipeline remains unchanged. Gemma/LoRA provides an additional experimental configuration; the new complexity score supports benchmark curation and evaluation rather than changing the proposed model or its inference procedure.

E1.justification: v3 introduces VisualTableQA: 306 held-out questions on tables from six existing seed datasets, curated to require reasoning over visual cues and tabular content. This adds a substantive capability requirement beyond the retained benchmarks, while the existing training instances remain unchanged (Sections 3.1–3.3 and Table 1).

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Gemma 3-4B zero-shot and MMTab-trained comparators. For the already evaluated Table Recognition task, v3 Table 10 adds DocOwl2, InternVL3-8B/14B, and Gemma-3-12B comparisons. Conversely, the one-shot comparator disappears from the held-out comparison in Table 4, although it remains in Table 3.

E3.justification: v3 adds Gemma 3-4B LoRA experiments, with quantized, one-epoch TABLET-M training documented in Appendix 12, and introduces complexity-based evaluation using 20 bins with sparse bins omitted. Appendix 8 also changes the stated gradient accumulation for 16-GPU runs from 4 to 8; this establishes a reported setting revision, not that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of performance across visual-complexity levels and robustness across backbone and training regime (Figure 2, Appendices 10–12). The earlier size and task-removal ablations remain, but much of the TABLET-B held-out visualization comparison in v2 Appendix 8.3 is removed.

E5.justification: v3 newly states that VisualTableQA results are averaged over three random seeds (Section 5). The existing bootstrap significance reporting at p < 0.05 is retained. Neither PDF establishes an increase in repeated runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds VisualTableQA scores, including TABLET-M 47.8%, zero-shot Qwen 42.4%, and MMTab 41.1%, plus Gemma fine-tuning and additional Table Recognition results. Earlier TABLET-B entries for TabMWP, TAT-QA, TabMCQ, AIT-QA, and PubHealthTab disappear. Table 2 changes the TABLET-B_synth WikiTQ original-image score from 56.5 to 56.4. Most retained Qwen scores and the relocated degradation scores are unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix 10 introduces a mathematically defined visual-complexity score, with component definitions, normalization rules, and a weighted aggregation in Equations 1–12. This is substantial new formal metric content, although it adds no learning-theoretic guarantees. The earlier degradation-score definition remains unchanged.

C1.justification: VisualTableQA becomes a principal contribution in the abstract and introduction, extending the paper's claims to joint visual and tabular reasoning on a newly introduced benchmark. v3 also explicitly includes Gemma fine-tuning and changes the stated state-of-the-art coverage from 10/14 to 11/15 benchmarks. The original dataset, extensibility, and transfer claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 emphasizes that existing benchmarks inadequately test visual information and explicitly cautions that mixed-training gains could reflect additional samples. v3 adds interpretations about transferable compositional visual reasoning, robustness across architectures and training regimes, and resilience to visual complexity. Its rewritten mixed-training discussion gives a more definite attribution to realism and scale, while the limitations section remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix 12 supplies detailed Gemma TABLET-M settings, including NF4 quantization, LoRA rank/alpha, trainable modules, optimizer, batch size, and learning rate. v3 also documents benchmark curation and complexity computation, revises Qwen gradient-accumulation information, and updates the dataset example's path fields and metadata structure (Figure 4).

R1.justification: The reference list is unchanged. Section 2 adds the specific criticism that TableVQA-Bench questions can be answered from textual content alone, sharpening the positioning of the new VisualTableQA benchmark.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract, contribution list, experimental questions, and visualization discussion, and shortens some dataset explanations. It adds acknowledgments and conference headers. These are focused narrative revisions; the main section order and most existing appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 2 consolidates original-image scores and previously separate degradation results into a revised display. Tables 3, 4, and the open-weight held-out table change structure. v3 adds complexity plots, a component-weight table, and VisualTableQA illustrations; existing task examples are largely retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses two important evidence gaps acknowledged in v2: benchmarks poorly suited to testing visual cues and reliance on one fine-tuned backbone. VisualTableQA provides direct evaluation with documented Qwen gains, while Gemma experiments and complexity analyses substantially strengthen the dataset's empirical foundation. These benefits outweigh the removed subsidiary results and reporting defects: the rewritten discussion reverses the HiTab/TabFact comparisons shown in Table 2, and Section 9 still incorrectly describes fine-tuning as limited to one model.
